# Reformat .RTF files

```{r}
# Load required packages

# Set the paths for your folders
input_folder <- "./Files_rtf/"  # Replace with your input folder path
output_folder <- "./file_raw_text/" # Replace with your output folder path

# Create output folder if it doesn't exist
if (!dir.exists(output_folder)) {
  dir.create(output_folder)
}

# Get a list of all .rtf files in the input folder
rtf_files <- list.files(path = input_folder, pattern = "\\.RTF$", full.names = TRUE)

# Convert each .rtf file to .txt
for (file in rtf_files) {
  # Extract the file name without extension
  file_name <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file))
  
  # Read the RTF content
  rtf_content <- read_rtf(file)
  
  # Create output file path
  output_file <- file.path(output_folder, paste0(file_name, ".txt"))
  
  # Write the content to a .txt file
  writeLines(rtf_content, output_file)
  
  # Print progress
  cat("Converted:", file, "to", output_file, "\n")
}

cat("Conversion complete!\n")
```
# Raw text compiler

```{r include=FALSE}
#This creates an index with the file path to the stories. And then it compiles the stories into a dataframe
#####################
# Begin SM Code #####
#####################

###
# List out text files that match pattern .txt, create DF
###

#Adjust thisline for your file name
files <- list.files("./file_raw_text", pattern="*.txt") %>% 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  rename(filename = 1) |> 
  #create an matching file name
  mutate(index = str_replace_all(filename, ".txt", "")) %>%
  mutate(index = tolower(gsub("[[:punct:][:space:]|]", "", index))) |> 
  mutate(index = tolower(index)) |> 
  mutate(index = str_sub(index, 1, 25)) |> 
  distinct(index, .keep_all = TRUE)


#Join the file list to the index

final_data <- rio::import("XJWM_list.XLSX") |> 
  clean_names() |> 
   #create an matching file name
  mutate(index = tolower(gsub("[[:punct:][:space:]|]", "", title))) |> 
  mutate(index = tolower(index)) |> 
  mutate(index = str_sub(index, 1, 25)) |> 
  distinct(index, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

#Text compiler

```{r}
###
# Define function to loop through each text file 
###

create_article_text <- function(row_value) {
  
  #row_value is the single argument that is passed to the function
  # Take each row of the dataframe
  temp <- final_index %>%
    slice(row_value)
  
  # Store the filename for  use in constructing articles dataframe
  temp_filename <- temp$filename
  
  # Create a dataframe by reading in lines of a given textfile
  # Add a filename column 
  articles_df_temp <- read_lines(temp$filepath) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(filename = temp_filename)
  
  # Bind results to master articles_df
  # <<- returns to global environment
  articles_df <<- articles_df %>%
    bind_rows(articles_df_temp)
}

###
# Create elements needed to run function
###

# Create empty tibble to store results
articles_df <- tibble()
#running once to test
#create_article_text(2) 
# Create an array of numbers to loop through, from 1 to the number of rows in our index dataframe 
row_values <- 1:nrow(final_index)

###
# Execute function using lapply
# This loops through each row of the dataframe and append results to master file
###

lapply(row_values, create_article_text)

###
# Clean up articles_df and join to index dataframe
###

articles_df <- articles_df %>%
  select(filename, sentence=value) %>%
  inner_join(final_index)


# write.csv(articles_df, "..articles_df.csv")

```

```{r}
bigrams
```

```{r}
data(stop_words)

bigrams1 <- bigrams %>%
  filter(!is.na(bigram)) |> 
  separate(bigram, c("word1", "word2"), sep = " ")

bigrams2 <- bigrams1 %>%
  filter(!word1 %in% stop_words$word) %>%
  filter(!word2 %in% stop_words$word) |> 
  count(word1, word2, sort = TRUE) |> 
  mutate(decade = "post2015") # label the range of your data

head(bigrams2, 100)
```

#Memo 307 words

The top 15 bigrams in my data do not add much to understanding the content. The top 3 bigrams refer to the Uyghur Autonomous Region of Xinjiang in China and repeat themselves in various combinations. Other location-related bigrams are "northwest china" and "xinjiang china". Among the top 10 bigrams, the combination of words "load date", "language english", and "publication type" also does not carry any value and should be removed. Only bigram #4, "human rights," carries some meaning and may indicate what the articles might mention, apart from the obvious location indicators. The next 10 bigrams (11-20) contain a bit more meaning and have combinations of words such as "right violations", "national security", "chinese government". However, bigrams such as "type newspaper", "journal code", "copyright 2021" and "china 94" should be cleaned out. The bigram "negative news" is an interesting outlier in this batch and may indicate articles flagged by the Chinese press as "negative coverage" of Xinjiang by the West. The next batch of bigrams (21-30) has such words as "birth control", "family planning", and "global times" that are most meaningful. The Global Times is a Chinese media outlet that is working under the auspices of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and frequently writes about denouncements and "lies" about Xinjiang. The bigrams "90 human", "region society", "research institute", "friendship association", "78 human", "china 93", and "beijing china" can also be cleaned out, as they do not add meaning to the articles. The bigrams batch 31-40 contains "ethnic minority", "human reproductive", "reproductive sterilization", "reproductive health", "ethnic conflicts" among the more or less meaningful combinations of words. The bigrams "china 96", "chinese embassy", "90 negative", "social media" and "united kingdom" can be cleaned out. Overall, the further you go into bigrams, the more meaningful the words become. However, the data needs substantial cleaning and contextual understanding for certain bigrams.
